title: 📚 Era 1 Works: Ancient & Classical World
subtitle: Verify publication dates, summaries, characters, storylines & exam traps for 89 works

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Iliad

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 750 BCE (Sort Year: -750)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Homer

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An epic of Achilles' anger in the last year of the Trojan War.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: About 750 BCE is the usual exam date for a late 8th century composition. Wikipedia also allows a date into the 7th century BCE. There was no print publication. Singers performed it.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Achilles (The greatest Greek fighter, whose anger drives the plot); Agamemnon (King of Mycenae and leader of the Greek armies); Hector (The chief Trojan prince, killed by Achilles); Patroclus (Achilles' dear companion, killed while wearing his armor); Priam (King of Troy, who ransoms Hector's body)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Referred as the Song of Ilion or Song of Ilium.
It is an ancient Greek epic poem in dactylic hexameter, set during Trojan War between King Agamemnon and the Warrior Achilles (15,693 lines). 3-Homeric Hymn: A collection of 33 anonymous ancient Greek Hymns celebrating individual god in dactylic hexameter. 4-Epic Cycle: A collection of ancient Greek epic poems that related the story of Trojan War which includes the Cypria, the Aethiopes, the so called Little Iliad, Ilupersis, the Nostoi and the Telegoni in dactylic hexameter.
Agamemnon takes Briseis, so Achilles refuses to fight.
The Greeks suffer until Patroclus dies in Achilles' armor.
Achilles returns, kills Hector, and mistreats the body.
Priam begs for his son, and Achilles returns the body.
The poem ends with Hector's funeral, not with Troy's fall.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Odyssey

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 725–675 BCE (Sort Year: -725)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Homer

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An epic of Odysseus fighting to reach home after the Trojan War.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates the writing to about 725 to 675 BCE. The exam date about 725 BCE is the start of that range.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Odysseus (King of Ithaca, trying to return home after Troy); Penelope (His wife, who delays the suitors for years); Telemachus (His son, who helps him kill the suitors); Athena (The goddess who guides Odysseus and Telemachus); Polyphemus (The Cyclops whom Odysseus blinds)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poem mainly focuses on the Greek hero Odysseus (known as Ulysses in Roman myths), king of Ithaca, and his journey home after the fall of Troy. It takes Odysseus ten years to reach Ithaca after the ten-year Trojan War. In his absence, it is assumed Odysseus has died, and his wife Penelope and son Telemachus must deal with a group of unruly suitors, the Mnesteres who compete for Penelope's hand in marriage.
George Chapman (1616) translated it to English.
It is written in dactylic hexameter.
It is sequel to the Iliad.
Telemachus looks for news while suitors fill the house.
Odysseus leaves Calypso and is shipwrecked among the Phaeacians.
He tells of the Cyclops, Circe, the dead, and the Sirens.
Athena disguises him in Ithaca, and he kills the suitors.
Penelope tests him with the secret of their marriage bed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Theogony

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 700 BCE (Sort Year: -700)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Hesiod

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poem on the birth of the gods and Zeus' rise to power.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and World History Encyclopedia place the poem about 700 BCE. It is often treated as Hesiod's earlier poem. There was no print publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Muses (Goddesses who give the poet his song on Mount Helicon); Zeus (The sky god who defeats Cronus and the Titans); Cronus (A Titan who overthrows his father and swallows his children); Prometheus (A Titan punished for tricking Zeus and helping humans)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Muses call the shepherd poet to sing on Helicon.
First come Chaos, Earth, Tartarus, and Desire.
Cronus overthrows his father, then swallows his own children.
Zeus escapes, defeats the Titans, and rules the gods.
The poem lists divine marriages and the birth of heroes.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Works and Days

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 700 BCE (Sort Year: -700)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Hesiod

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A farmer's poem on just work, the ages of man, and the lucky days.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and World History Encyclopedia date the poem about 700 BCE, with the Theogony.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hesiod (The farmer poet who advises his brother); Perses (The brother who disputed the family land); Pandora (The first woman, whose coming releases evils among humans); Zeus (The god who orders work and watches justice)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poet tells his brother Perses to stop cheating and work.
Prometheus' trick brings Pandora, and evils enter human life.
Five ages decline from gold toward the hard iron age.
The poet gives a calendar for plowing, sailing, and harvest.
He ends with days that are lucky or unlucky for tasks.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Surviving lyric poems / fragments

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 600 BCE (Sort Year: -600)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sappho

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Short lyric poems and fragments on love, friends, and Aphrodite, sung to the lyre.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Individual poems vary. No ancient publication year survives. The Hymn to Aphrodite is the one poem usually judged complete.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sappho (The poet speaker of the personal lyrics); Aphrodite (The love goddess addressed in the Hymn to Aphrodite)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Most of the nine ancient books of her poems are lost.
What remains are fragments on papyrus and lines quoted by later writers.
The Hymn to Aphrodite asks the goddess to ease a lover's pain.
Another famous fragment says a beloved person seems equal to the gods.
The poems were made to be sung, not read in silence.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Epinician Odes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 498-446 BCE (Sort Year: -498)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Pindar

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Choral victory songs praising athletes at the four great Greek games.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database range about 498 to 446 BCE matches the datable odes. Pythian 10 is the earliest, from 498 BCE. The last datable ode is from 446 BCE. Each ode has its own year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet (The speaker who praises the victor and tells the myth); The victor (The athlete, or his family, honored by the ode); The chorus (The singers and dancers who perform the ode)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A winner at the games, or his family, asked Pindar for a song.
A chorus sang and danced the ode for the victor's home or city.
The poet praises the winner, then turns to a myth.
The myth carries a warning about pride, luck, and the gods.
The song returns to the victor and wishes his house well.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Olympian odes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 476 BCE (Sort Year: -476)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Pindar

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The book of victory odes for winners at the Olympic games, including Olympian 1.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Olympian odes belong to the fifth century BCE, inside the larger epinician set. Olympian 1 celebrates the victory of 476 BCE. Other odes in the book have their own years.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Pindar (The poet who sings the horse song for Hieron); Hieron (Ruler of Syracuse, winner of the single horse race in 476 BCE); Pelops (The mythic hero whose Olympic fame the ode retells)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This book holds odes for winners at the Olympic games.
Olympian 1 praises Hieron of Syracuse for a horse victory in 476 BCE.
It opens by ranking water, then gold, then the Olympic games.
The myth retells how Pelops won his bride at Pisa.
Pindar tells Hieron not to reach past a king's proper height.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Oresteia

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 458 BCE (Sort Year: -458)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aeschylus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A trilogy in which revenge killings in the house of Atreus end in a court of law.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and Britannica both date the trilogy to 458 BCE. It was his last production in Athens.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Agamemnon (The king who returns from Troy and is murdered); Clytemnestra (His wife, who kills him and is later killed by their son); Orestes (The son who avenges his father and then stands trial); Electra (The daughter who helps Orestes plan the revenge); Athena (The goddess who founds the court and breaks the tie)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In Agamemnon, Clytemnestra kills her husband when he comes home from Troy.
In The Libation Bearers, their son Orestes kills her to avenge his father.
The Furies then hunt Orestes for the murder of his mother.
In The Eumenides, Athena sets a trial of citizens in Athens.
The votes are equal, Athena frees Orestes, and the Furies become protectors of the city.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Persians

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 472 BCE (Sort Year: -472)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aeschylus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The Persian court learns that Xerxes has lost his fleet at Salamis.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and Britannica both date the first performance to 472 BCE. It won first prize. Pericles was the sponsor.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Atossa (The queen mother of Xerxes, who receives the news); The Messenger (The man who reports the Greek victory at Salamis); Darius (The ghost of the former king, who blames his son's pride); Xerxes (The defeated king, who returns in ruin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In Susa, the Persian elders fear for the army of Xerxes.
Queen Atossa hears a messenger tell of the disaster at Salamis.
She calls up the ghost of the dead king Darius.
Darius says the defeat punishes the pride of his son.
Xerxes returns in rags, and the chorus laments with him.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Seven Against Thebes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 467 BCE (Sort Year: -467)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aeschylus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Eteocles defends Thebes against his brother Polyneices, and the brothers kill each other.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and Britannica both date the performance to 467 BCE. It won first prize. A later ending about Antigone was added after the lifetime of Aeschylus.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Eteocles (The king of Thebes, who dies fighting his own brother); Polyneices (The brother who attacks the city to claim the throne); The Spy (The man who describes each attacker at the gates); Chorus of Theban women (The frightened women of the city)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Polyneices brings six allied chiefs to attack the seven gates of Thebes.
Eteocles matches a defender to each gate.
He chooses the seventh gate himself, where his brother will fight.
The brothers kill each other, and the curse of Oedipus is fulfilled.
The city is saved, but the royal house is ruined.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Suppliants

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 463 BCE (Sort Year: -463)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aeschylus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The daughters of Danaus flee a forced marriage and beg Argos for protection.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A papyrus shows that the set competed against Sophocles, so it is not a very early play. Wikipedia heads the play at 463 BCE. Britannica says it was probably staged in 463 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Danaids (The chorus of daughters who beg for asylum); Danaus (Their father, who advises them how to plead); Pelasgus (The king of Argos, who puts the choice to his people)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The fifty daughters of Danaus flee Egypt to avoid marrying their cousins.
They supplicate King Pelasgus at Argos and threaten suicide at the altar.
Pelasgus will not decide alone, and he asks the people of Argos.
The people vote to protect the women.
A herald from Egypt demands them back, and war is near as the play ends.

items.title: "Prometheus Bound" (date disputed; commonly c. 460–450 BCE) — Aeschylus

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Prometheus Bound

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: date disputed; commonly c. 460–450 BCE (Sort Year: -460)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aeschylus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Zeus has Prometheus chained to a rock because Prometheus gave fire to humans.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The date and even the author are disputed. Britannica treats it as a late play if it is his. Wikipedia records guesses from the 480s BCE into the 410s BCE. The database says the date is disputed and commonly about 460 to 450 BCE. Do not treat the 450s as a fixed fact.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Prometheus (The Titan punished for giving fire and skill to humans); Hephaestus (The god who is forced to chain Prometheus); Io (The woman driven across the world by a jealous Hera); Hermes (The messenger who demands the secret and is refused)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hephaestus chains Prometheus to a cliff, though he pities him.
Prometheus says he saved humans and gave them fire and the arts.
Oceanus advises surrender, and Prometheus refuses.
Io, another victim of Zeus, hears a prophecy of her long wandering.
Prometheus will not reveal a secret that threatens Zeus, and he is cast into the abyss.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Agamemnon

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 458 BCE (Sort Year: -458)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aeschylus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Clytemnestra welcomes Agamemnon home from Troy and murders him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It was staged in 458 BCE as the first play of the Oresteia. Wikipedia and Britannica agree.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Agamemnon (The victorious king who is killed in his bath); Clytemnestra (The queen who plans the murder and defends it); Cassandra (The Trojan prophet who sees the killing and is not believed); Aegisthus (The lover of Clytemnestra and cousin of Agamemnon); Chorus of Argive elders (Old men who fear the house and cannot stop the crime)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A beacon tells Argos that Troy has fallen.
The chorus remembers how Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia.
Clytemnestra greets him with honor and leads him inside on purple cloth.
Cassandra, his captive, foresees his death and her own, then enters.
Clytemnestra displays the bodies and claims the killing as justice.
Aegisthus joins her rule.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Eumenides

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 458 BCE (Sort Year: -458)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aeschylus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Athena tries Orestes in Athens and turns the Furies into kindly guardians of the city.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It closed the Oresteia in 458 BCE. Wikipedia and Britannica agree. The name Eumenides means the Kindly Ones.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Orestes (The accused son, who is cleared of the killing); The Furies (The chorus of avengers, later renamed the Kindly Ones); Apollo (The god who ordered the killing and defends Orestes); Athena (The goddess who founds the court and breaks the tie)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Orestes seeks refuge at Delphi, and Apollo sends him on to Athens.
The Furies track him and demand punishment for his mother's blood.
Athena forms a jury of citizens to judge the case.
The votes tie, and Athena casts the vote that frees him.
She persuades the Furies to stay as the Eumenides, the Kindly Ones, and bless Athens.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Libation Bearers

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 458 BCE (Sort Year: -458)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aeschylus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Orestes returns from exile and kills Clytemnestra and Aegisthus.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It was staged in 458 BCE with Agamemnon and The Eumenides. Wikipedia and Britannica agree.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Orestes (The son who avenges Agamemnon and is then pursued); Electra (The daughter who recognizes him and shares the plan); Clytemnestra (The mother who is killed at Apollo's command); Aegisthus (Her lover, killed first); Chorus of slave women (The libation bearers who urge the revenge)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Orestes prays at the tomb of Agamemnon and meets his sister Electra.
Clytemnestra has sent Electra with libations (drink offerings) because of a bad dream.
Orestes enters the palace with a false report of his own death.
He kills Aegisthus, then kills his mother.
The Furies appear to him, and he flees in madness.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Ajax

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 445 BCE (Sort Year: -445)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sophocles

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The warrior Ajax kills himself after losing the armor of Achilles.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: No official festival record fixes the year. The play is usually called early. Estimates often fall between about 450 and 440 BCE. One study suggests about 445 BCE. The database prints a range, about 450 to 440 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ajax (A proud Greek warrior who kills himself after public shame); Tecmessa (The captive woman who loves Ajax and begs him to live); Teucer (The half brother of Ajax, who fights for his burial); Odysseus (The rival who later defends the right of Ajax to burial); Athena (The goddess who shows Odysseus the madness of Ajax)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After Achilles dies, his armor is given to Odysseus, not to Ajax.
Mad with shame, Ajax kills sheep, thinking they are the Greek chiefs.
When his mind clears, he cannot bear the disgrace, and he kills himself.
His brother Teucer wants to bury him, but the chiefs refuse at first.
Odysseus argues for a proper burial, and the chiefs at last agree.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Antigone

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 441 BCE (Sort Year: -441)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sophocles

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Antigone buries her brother against the order of King Creon and dies for it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Ancient evidence points to 442 or 441 BCE. Britannica and Wikipedia both give that window. A story links the play to his election as general, but that link is doubtful.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Antigone (The daughter of Oedipus, who buries her brother and accepts death); Creon (The king of Thebes, whose rigid order destroys his own family); Ismene (The sister who fears the law and will not help at first); Haemon (The son of Creon and the betrothed of Antigone); Tiresias (The blind prophet who warns Creon that the gods are angry)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Creon forbids burial for Polyneices, who attacked his own city.
Antigone buries her brother because divine law outranks the king's order.
Creon condemns her, and he refuses the warnings of his son Haemon.
The blind prophet Tiresias says the city is polluted by the unburied corpse.
Creon yields too late.
Antigone, Haemon, and Queen Eurydice are dead.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Histories

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 430 BCE (Sort Year: -430)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Herodotus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prose history of the wars between Greece and Persia, and of the peoples drawn into them.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Perseus dates the finish about 430 BCE. Britannica says the latest event belongs to 430 BCE, and the work was known in Athens before 425 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Herodotus (The narrator who inquires, travels, and records what he is told); Croesus (King of Lydia, whose fall opens the rise of Persia); Xerxes (Persian king who leads the great invasion of Greece)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Herodotus sets out to save great deeds of Greeks and other peoples from being forgotten.
He traces how Persia grew under Cyrus, Cambyses, and Darius.
He describes Egypt, Scythia, and many other lands along the way.
The last books tell how Xerxes invaded Greece.
Greek victories at Salamis, Plataea, and Mycale close the war in 480 and 479 BCE.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Alcestis

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 438 BCE (Sort Year: -438)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Euripides

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Alcestis dies in place of her husband Admetus, and Heracles brings her back.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and Britannica both date the performance to 438 BCE. It took second prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Alcestis (The wife who dies so her husband may live); Admetus (The king who accepts her death and then grieves); Heracles (The hero who saves Alcestis from Death); Pheres (The father of Admetus, who refuses to die for his son)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Admetus may live if someone else will die for him.
His parents refuse.
His wife Alcestis agrees and dies.
Admetus learns too late how empty his house will be.
His friend Heracles arrives, learns the truth, and wrestles Death.
Heracles returns Alcestis alive, and the house is restored.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Medea

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 431 BCE (Sort Year: -431)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Euripides

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Medea kills the new bride of Jason, and then kills her own two sons.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and Britannica both date the performance to 431 BCE. The set placed third. Euphorion, son of Aeschylus, won.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Medea (The foreign wife who answers betrayal with killing); Jason (The hero who abandons her for a royal marriage); Creon (The king of Corinth, who exiles her and then dies); The Nurse (The servant who fears what Medea may do); Aegeus (The king of Athens, who offers Medea a refuge)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jason leaves Medea to marry the princess of Corinth.
Medea wins one more day in the city and plans her revenge.
She sends poisoned gifts, and the princess and the king die.
After a terrible struggle, she kills her two sons.
She escapes in the chariot of the sun, and Jason is left with nothing.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Oedipus Rex

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 429 BCE (Sort Year: -429)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sophocles

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: King Oedipus hunts the killer of Laius and finds that he himself is the killer.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia gives a premiere about 429 BCE, but calls the year highly uncertain. The database prints about 429 to 425 BCE. No official record survives. Do not treat 429 BCE as a fixed fact.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Oedipus (The king of Thebes, who discovers that he is the source of the plague); Jocasta (The queen, who is both his wife and his mother); Creon (The brother of Jocasta, sent to ask the oracle for help); Tiresias (The blind prophet who says Oedipus himself is the killer); The Shepherd (The man who once saved the baby Oedipus and later tells the truth)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A plague strikes Thebes, and the oracle says the killer of Laius must be punished.
Oedipus curses the unknown killer and quarrels with the prophet Tiresias.
He learns that he was a foundling, and that he killed a man at a crossroads.
The truth comes out.
He has killed his father and married his mother, Jocasta.
Jocasta hangs herself.
Oedipus blinds himself and asks to be sent away.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hippolytus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 428 BCE (Sort Year: -428)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Euripides

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Phaedra loves her stepson Hippolytus, and a false charge leads Theseus to destroy him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and Britannica both date this performance to 428 BCE. It won first prize. An earlier Hippolytus is lost.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hippolytus (The chaste son who scorns Aphrodite and is destroyed); Phaedra (The queen destroyed by a love she is ashamed to feel); Theseus (The father who curses his son on a false charge); Aphrodite (The goddess who opens the play and sets the punishment); Artemis (The goddess who tells the truth at the end)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Aphrodite punishes Hippolytus because he honors only the virgin Artemis.
She makes Phaedra, wife of Theseus, fall in love with her stepson.
The truth is told to him.
He rejects her, and she hangs herself.
Her letter falsely accuses him.
Theseus calls down a curse.
A bull from the sea kills Hippolytus.
Artemis reveals the truth before he dies.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Knights

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 424 BCE (Sort Year: -424)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aristophanes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A sausage seller outdoes the politician Cleon as the servant of the people.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia, Perseus, and Britannica date the play to 424 BCE, at the Lenaea. It won first prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Demos (A grumpy old man who stands for the Athenian people); The Paphlagonian (A slave who represents the politician Cleon); The Sausage Seller (A cruder man who wins the favor of Demos); Chorus of Knights (Wealthy cavalrymen who hate Cleon)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Demos, a figure of the Athenian people, is ruled by a slave called the Paphlagonian.
That slave stands for Cleon, the powerful popular leader.
Two other slaves find a sausage seller who can shout even louder.
The sausage seller beats Cleon in a contest of flattery and abuse.
Demos is boiled young again, and he rejects the bad leader.

items.title: "History of the Peloponnesian War" (c. 431-411 BCE) — Thucydides

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: History of the Peloponnesian War

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 431-411 BCE (Sort Year: -431)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Thucydides

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unfinished prose history of the war between Athens and Sparta, written by a man who fought in it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database span about 423 to 400 BCE is only a rough mark, and the unfinished flag is correct. He began near the outbreak in 431 BCE. The narrative breaks off in 411 BCE. He probably died about 400 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thucydides (The Athenian general who narrates and explains the war); Pericles (Athenian leader whose Funeral Oration praises the city); The Athenians at Melos (Speakers who argue that power, not justice, rules between unequals); The Melians (Leaders of neutral Melos who plead for their freedom)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Athens and Sparta begin a great war in 431 BCE.
Thucydides explains the power and fear that caused it.
Pericles praises Athens in the Funeral Oration for the first dead.
In the Melian Dialogue, Athens tells neutral Melos that the strong rule.
The text breaks off in 411 BCE, before Athens loses the war.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Clouds

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 423 BCE (Sort Year: -423)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aristophanes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A father sends his son to the thought shop of Socrates in order to escape his debts.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The first version was staged in 423 BCE and did poorly. The text we have is an unfinished revision from about 419 to 416 BCE. Perseus and Wikipedia say that revision was never staged. The database is right to flag the surviving text as revised.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Strepsiades (The debtor who wants dishonest arguments); Pheidippides (His son, who learns the new logic and beats him); Socrates (A comic version of the philosopher, shown as a sophist); Chorus of Clouds (Goddesses of the new learning)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Strepsiades is ruined by the debts of his horse loving son.
He goes to the Thinkery, where Socrates hangs in a basket.
He wants to learn how to make the worse case sound better.
His son learns instead, and then beats his father and defends the act.
Strepsiades burns the Thinkery down.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Wasps

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 422 BCE (Sort Year: -422)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aristophanes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A son tries to cure his father of a mad love of serving on juries.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia, Perseus, and Britannica date the play to 422 BCE, at the Lenaea.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Philocleon (The old juror whose name means Love Cleon); Bdelycleon (The son whose name means Loathe Cleon); Chorus of Wasps (Old jurors who sting like wasps)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Old Philocleon lives to sit on juries and collect the jury pay.
His son Bdelycleon locks him in the house.
The chorus of old jurors, dressed as wasps, comes to free him.
The son sets up a mock court at home, and the house dog is tried for stealing cheese.
Philocleon leaves the courts, but he then becomes a wild drunk.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Electra

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 410 BCE (Sort Year: -410)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sophocles

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Electra and Orestes kill their mother Clytemnestra to avenge their father Agamemnon.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: No official record survives. Style puts the play late in his career. Estimates often run from about 420 to 410 BCE. The database prints about 420 to 410 BCE. The year 410 BCE is a late estimate, not a fixed fact.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Electra (The daughter who lives for revenge and will not be calmed); Orestes (The exiled son who returns in secret to kill the killers); Clytemnestra (The mother who killed Agamemnon and is killed in turn); Chrysothemis (The cautious sister who refuses to join the plot); Aegisthus (The lover of Clytemnestra, killed after she dies)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Electra mourns Agamemnon and hates Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus.
She thinks Orestes is dead after a false report and an urn of ashes.
Orestes reveals himself, and the brother and sister plan the killing.
Orestes kills Clytemnestra inside the house while Electra urges him on.
Aegisthus is then led in to die, and the revenge is complete.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Trojan Women

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 415 BCE (Sort Year: -415)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Euripides

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: After Troy falls, Hecuba and the other women are shared out as slaves.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and Britannica both date the performance to 415 BCE. It was part of a set that placed second. It followed the Athenian killing of the men of Melos.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hecuba (The old queen who suffers each new loss in turn); Cassandra (The prophet daughter, taken as the prize of Agamemnon); Andromache (The widow of Hector, whose small son is killed); Helen (The woman blamed for the war, who argues for her life); Talthybius (The Greek herald who brings each cruel order)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Troy has fallen.
The gods plan further pain for the Greek victors.
Hecuba learns that Cassandra must go with Agamemnon.
Andromache is given to Neoptolemus, and her son Astyanax is taken to die.
Helen defends herself before Menelaus, and Hecuba answers her.
Astyanax is buried, Troy is burned, and the women are led to the ships.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Birds

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 414 BCE (Sort Year: -414)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aristophanes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two Athenians persuade the birds to found a city in the sky and blockade the gods.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia, Perseus, and the Loeb chronology date the play to 414 BCE, at the City Dionysia. It took second prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Peisetairus (The clever Athenian who founds the bird city); Euelpides (His companion, hopeful and less cunning); Chorus of Birds (The birds who become a new power between earth and heaven)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Peisetairus and Euelpides leave Athens, tired of lawsuits.
They meet the birds and propose a city in the air.
The new city is called Cloudcuckooland.
It blocks the smoke of sacrifices, so the gods grow hungry.
The gods yield.
Peisetairus marries the divine princess and rules.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Electra

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 413 BCE (Sort Year: -413)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Euripides

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Electra, married to a poor farmer, helps Orestes kill their mother.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: No official record fixes the year. The database prints about 413 BCE. Britannica places the play about 418 BCE. A chronology on Wikipedia places it about 420 BCE. All of these are estimates. Do not treat 413 BCE as a fixed fact.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Electra (The bitter daughter who pushes the killing of her mother); Orestes (The brother who strikes, then cannot bear what he has done); Clytemnestra (The mother who comes to help and is killed); The Farmer (The poor husband who has not touched Electra); Castor (A god who appears at the end and gives commands)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Electra lives in a farmer's hut, kept from a royal marriage.
Orestes returns in secret and is recognized at the hut.
Electra lures Clytemnestra to the hut with a false story of a birth.
Orestes kills Aegisthus at a sacrifice, then kills his mother.
Brother and sister are filled with horror.
The gods send them apart.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Lysistrata

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 411 BCE (Sort Year: -411)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aristophanes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Lysistrata leads the women of Greece to refuse sex until the men make peace.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia, Perseus, and the Loeb chronology date the play to 411 BCE, at the Lenaea. Athens was in crisis after the Sicilian defeat.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lysistrata (The Athenian woman who organizes the sex strike); Calonice (An Athenian wife who hesitates, then joins); Myrrhine (A wife who teases her desperate husband); Lampito (The Spartan woman who brings the other side in); Chorus of old men (Men who try and fail to retake the Acropolis)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lysistrata gathers women from Athens and from enemy cities.
They swear to refuse their husbands until the war ends.
The older women seize the treasury on the Acropolis.
The sex strike and the seizure of the money force the men to talk.
A peace is made, and the couples are reunited.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Philoctetes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 409 BCE (Sort Year: -409)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sophocles

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Odysseus and Neoptolemus must bring the wounded Philoctetes and his bow back to Troy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The year is firm. Wikipedia and Britannica both place the first performance in 409 BCE. It won first prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Philoctetes (The abandoned archer whose bow the Greeks need); Neoptolemus (The son of Achilles, caught between orders and honesty); Odysseus (The planner who wants the bow by a trick); Heracles (The hero who appears at the end and commands the voyage to Troy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Greeks once left Philoctetes on Lemnos because a snake bite made him foul.
A prophecy now says Troy cannot fall without his bow.
Odysseus tells young Neoptolemus to trick Philoctetes and steal the bow.
Neoptolemus pities him, returns the bow, and refuses the dishonest plan.
Heracles appears and orders Philoctetes to sail to Troy and be healed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Iphigenia in Aulis

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 405 BCE (Sort Year: -405)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Euripides

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Agamemnon must sacrifice his daughter Iphigenia at Aulis before the fleet can sail.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Euripides died in 406 BCE. The play was staged in 405 BCE with The Bacchae, and the prize was given after his death. His son may have finished the script. Wikipedia notes later additions in the text. The database calls it posthumous, about 405 BCE, and that performance year is right.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Iphigenia (The daughter who comes for a wedding and accepts death); Agamemnon (The general who cannot escape the sacrifice); Clytemnestra (The mother who learns the trick and pleads for her child); Achilles (The hero whose name was used in the false marriage); Menelaus (The brother who wants the war to proceed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The army is stuck at Aulis, and the seer demands the death of Iphigenia.
Agamemnon has summoned her with a false promise of marriage to Achilles.
He wavers, and Menelaus and Clytemnestra fight over the girl.
Achilles offers to defend her, but the army wants the sacrifice.
Iphigenia chooses to die for Greece, and she is led to the altar.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Bacchae

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 405 BCE (Sort Year: -405)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Euripides

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: King Pentheus rejects the god Dionysus and is torn apart by the women of Thebes.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Euripides died in 406 BCE. The Bacchae was staged in 405 BCE with Iphigenia in Aulis. The prize was posthumous. Wikipedia and the life in Britannica agree on that production.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dionysus (The god who comes in human form and punishes Thebes); Pentheus (The young king who mocks the god and is destroyed); Agave (The mother who kills her son while possessed); Cadmus (The old founder who must bring Agave back to sense); Chorus of Bacchae (Asian women who worship Dionysus)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dionysus comes to Thebes in disguise because the city denies his worship.
King Pentheus insults the god and tries to lock him up.
The god escapes and maddens the women on the mountain.
Pentheus is dressed as a woman and led out to spy on them.
His mother Agave, in a frenzy, kills him and carries his head home.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Frogs

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 405 BCE (Sort Year: -405)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aristophanes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Dionysus goes to the underworld to bring a dead tragic poet back to Athens.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia, Perseus, and the Loeb chronology date the play to 405 BCE, at the Lenaea. It won first prize. Athens ordered a second performance.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dionysus (The god of drama, who judges the dead poets); Xanthias (His slave, who swaps roles with him for the jokes); Aeschylus (The dead poet who speaks for the old, weighty style); Euripides (The dead poet who speaks for the clever new style); Chorus of Frogs (The frogs of the lake, famous for their croak)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dionysus misses good tragedy and sets out to fetch Euripides from Hades.
He crosses the lake while a frog chorus croaks.
In Hades he finds Euripides challenging Aeschylus for the chair of tragedy.
The two poets weigh lines, and Aeschylus wins the contest.
Dionysus chooses Aeschylus to return, as the poet Athens needs.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Oedipus at Colonus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 401 BCE (Sort Year: -401)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Sophocles

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The blind exile Oedipus finds a holy death at Colonus, under the protection of Athens.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Sophocles died in 406 BCE. His grandson staged the play in 401 BCE. Wikipedia and Britannica both call that performance posthumous. The database tag for a posthumous first performance is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Oedipus (The blind former king, now a wanderer seeking a holy death); Antigone (The daughter who guides her father in exile); Ismene (The other daughter, who brings news of the oracle); Theseus (The king of Athens, who grants Oedipus protection); Creon (The ruler of Thebes, who tries to seize Oedipus by force)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Blind Oedipus and his daughter Antigone reach Colonus, near Athens.
A prophecy says the place of his death will bless the city that holds him.
King Theseus protects him from Creon, who tries to drag him back.
Oedipus refuses to help his son Polyneices, who is marching on Thebes.
Oedipus walks to a secret place and dies in peace.
Only Theseus knows the spot.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Apology

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 399-387 BCE (Sort Year: -399)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Plato

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Socrates defends his life and teaching before an Athenian jury.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The trial is 399 BCE. The dialogue was written soon after, in Plato's early years. The database span is about 399 to 390 BCE. Both point to that early period.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Socrates (The philosopher on trial, who speaks his own defense); Meletus (One of the three men who accused Socrates)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Socrates speaks at his trial for impiety in 399 BCE.
He says old comic slander, especially Aristophanes, turned the city against him.
He explains the oracle that called him the wisest man.
He questions Meletus and says he will not stop philosophizing.
The jury condemns him, and he accepts death rather than exile.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Ion

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 390 BCE (Sort Year: -390)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Plato

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Socrates tells a rhapsode that poetry comes from divine inspiration, not skill.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Ion is an early dialogue. The database gives about 390 to 380 BCE. The exam date used here is about 390 BCE. No finer year is fixed.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Socrates (The questioner who tests Ion's claim to knowledge); Ion of Ephesus (A prize winning rhapsode who recites and explains Homer)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ion, a rhapsode (a performer of epic), boasts that he knows Homer best.
Socrates asks why that skill fails for other poets.
He says poets and rhapsodes speak by divine possession, not by art.
He compares inspiration to a magnet passing force along a chain.
Ion must choose between real knowledge and divine inspiration.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Symposium

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 385-370 BCE (Sort Year: -385)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Plato

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Athenian guests at a drinking party give speeches in praise of love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates the Symposium about 385 to 370 BCE. The database uses the same span. A narrower guess is about 385 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Socrates (The philosopher who reports Diotima's teaching on love); Diotima (A wise woman whose speech describes the ladder of love); Aristophanes (The comic poet who tells the myth of split humans); Alcibiades (A brilliant Athenian who arrives drunk and praises Socrates)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Friends meet at Agathon's house to praise Eros, the god of love.
Each guest offers a different speech about what love is.
Aristophanes tells a myth of humans split in half.
Socrates reports Diotima's ladder, rising from bodies to the Form of Beauty.
Alcibiades bursts in and praises Socrates as the true lover of wisdom.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Republic

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 375 BCE (Sort Year: -375)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Plato

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Socrates builds an ideal city to define justice, and Book 10 attacks poetry.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates the Republic to about 375 BCE. The database says about 380 BCE. Both place it in Plato's middle years. Book 10 is the criticism set piece.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Socrates (The main speaker who designs the just city and criticizes poetry); Glaucon (Plato's brother, who pushes Socrates to defend justice); Adeimantus (Plato's brother, who also challenges Socrates on justice)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Republic (Latin: De La Republica) is a Socratic dialogue written by Plato around 380 BC.
It concerns with the 'definition of justice', 'the order and character of the just city- state' and 'the just man' for this reason ancient readers used the name "On Justice" as an alternative title.
It's proved to be most influential works of philosophy and political theory. In it Socrates along with various Athenians and foreigners discusses the meaning of justice and examine whether or not 'the just man' is happier than 'the unjust man', by considering a series of different cities coming into existence "in speech" culminating in a city "Kallipolis" which is ruled by philosopher kings.
The participants also discuss The Theory of Forms, the immortality of the soul and the roles of the philosopher and of poetry in society.
It is written in 10 books.
Socrates defines 'Timocracy' as a government of people who love, rule and honour.
The Republic was well distinguished along with Parmenides, Phaedrus and Theaetetus.
In this work Plato recommended only two musical modes , they are Lydian and Ionian.
Socrates asks what justice is, in the soul and in the city.
He designs a city with rulers, guards, and workers.
The rulers should be philosopher kings who know the Good.
The cave story shows people mistaking shadows for reality.
Book 10 says imitative poetry is thrice removed from truth, so most poets are banished.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Phaedrus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 370 BCE (Sort Year: -370)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Plato

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Socrates and Phaedrus discuss love, rhetoric, and the weakness of writing.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates the Phaedrus to about 370 BCE, near the Republic and the Symposium. The database agrees. Aristotle's Rhetoric page also gives about 370 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Socrates (The main speaker on love, the soul, rhetoric, and writing); Phaedrus (A young man who brings Lysias's written speech)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Phaedrus reads a speech on love by the orator Lysias.
Socrates answers with speeches on love and the soul.
He pictures the soul as a charioteer with two horses.
He says true rhetoric must know the souls it addresses.
He argues that writing is only a reminder, while living talk can answer questions.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Politics

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 335-323 BCE (Sort Year: -335)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aristotle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A study of the city, constitutions, and the best life in a community.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The text mentions the killing of Philip of Macedon in 336 BCE. So part of it is later than that year. It belongs to the Lyceum years, 335 to 322 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aristotle (The lecturer whose notes form the treatise)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Aristotle says the city is the highest human community.
He calls the human being a political animal by nature.
He criticizes the shared property and shared families in Plato's Republic.
He sorts constitutions by who rules and by whether they serve the common good.
He discusses how cities stay stable or fall into revolution.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Rhetoric

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 335-322 BCE (Sort Year: -335)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aristotle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A treatise on persuasion, the types of speech, and style.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Rhetoric grew in two Athens periods, 367 to 347 BCE and 335 to 322 BCE. The exam span is the Lyceum years. The database starts the span at about 350 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aristotle (The lecturer whose notes form the treatise)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Aristotle calls rhetoric the counterpart of dialectic.
He names three kinds of speech: political, courtroom, and ceremonial.
A speaker persuades by ethos, pathos, and logos.
Book 2 studies emotions and types of listeners.
Book 3 treats style, metaphor, and the order of a speech.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Nicomachean Ethics

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 340 BCE (Sort Year: -340)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aristotle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A treatise on happiness, virtue, and the mean in human character.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: One passage mentions a battle of 353 BCE, so that part is later than 353. W. D. Ross placed the whole work in the Athens years 335 to 322 BCE. The exam date stays about 340 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aristotle (The lecturer whose notes form the treatise)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Aristotle asks what the highest human good is.
He calls that good eudaimonia (a flourishing life).
Moral virtue is a habit that hits the mean between extremes.
He studies courage, temperance, justice, and friendship.
The best life includes contemplation as well as practical wisdom.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poetics

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 335 BCE (Sort Year: -335)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Aristotle

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The first surviving treatise on poetry, focused on tragedy and epic.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates the Poetics to about 335 BCE, in the Lyceum years. The database agrees. Only the book on tragedy and epic survives.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aristotle (The lecturer whose notes form the treatise)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the earliest surviving work of dramatic theory. It has 26 chapters .
Aristotle works on aesthetics, consist of Poetic and Rhetoric. The poetics is especially concerned with drama.
Aristotle argued that poetry provides a safe outlet for the release of intense emotions.
The followers of Aristotle later known as Peripatetics.
Aristotle was the teacher of Alexander the Great.
In it he said that "tragedy is the imitation of an action that is complete and whole and of a certain magnitude having a beginning a middle and an end.
He also coined the term 'Entelechy' that means anything which is currently happening.
Aristotle says poetry is mimesis, imitation of human action.
Tragedy imitates a serious, complete action of some size.
It should arouse pity and fear and bring catharsis of those feelings.
The best tragic plot turns on hamartia, a mistake, plus reversal and recognition.
He ranks six parts, with plot first and spectacle last.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Idylls

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 270 BCE (Sort Year: -270)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Theocritus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Short poems of shepherds, town life, and court praise, including the first pastoral elegy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Other idylls vary. No single year covers the whole book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thyrsis (The singer who laments Daphnis in Idyll 1); Daphnis (The herdsman who dies of love in the first pastoral elegy); The goatherd (The listener who asks Thyrsis for the song of Daphnis)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Shepherds and goatherds meet in the countryside.
They sing of love, and they hold singing contests.
In Idyll 1, Thyrsis laments the dying herdsman Daphnis.
Daphnis dies of love rather than yield to Aphrodite.
Later poets copied this lament in the pastoral elegy.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Argonautica

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 3rd century BCE (Sort Year: -250)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Apollonius of Rhodes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A four book epic on Jason, the Argonauts, the Golden Fleece, and Medea's love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The poem belongs to the third century BCE. Britannica places his librarianship about 260 to 247 BCE, the age when the epic was composed.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jason (Leader of the Argonauts, sent to bring back the Golden Fleece); Medea (Princess of Colchis whose love and magic save Jason); Pelias (King who sends Jason on the dangerous quest); Heracles (A hero who joins the voyage and then leaves it)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
King Pelias sends Jason to fetch the Golden Fleece.
Jason gathers heroes, and the ship Argo sails toward Colchis.
In Book 3, the goddesses make Medea fall in love with Jason.
Medea's magic helps Jason win the fleece and escape.
The lovers sail back toward Greece, and the voyage tests their bond.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Epigrams

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 3rd century BCE (Sort Year: -250)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Callimachus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: About sixty short poems on tombs, gifts, love, and the craft of poetry.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Individual epigrams vary. No single year can be fixed for the whole set.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet (The first person speaker of many epigrams)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
An epigram is a short poem, once cut on stone or a gift.
Callimachus wrote at least sixty epigrams on many subjects.
Some are for the dead, and some are offerings to gods.
Others speak of love or of how a poem should be written.
Most survive because later anthologies copied them.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Hymns

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 3rd century BCE (Sort Year: -250)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Callimachus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Six learned hymns to Greek gods, mixing ritual voices with rare myth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Exact years for each hymn vary. All six belong to his Alexandrian career.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet celebrant (The speaker who calls the god and guides the hymn); Zeus (God of the first hymn, praised through the story of his birth); Apollo (God of poetry, addressed in a hymn staged like a rite)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Six hymns address Zeus, Apollo, Artemis, Delos, Athena, and Demeter.
Each hymn calls on a god and tells a story of that god.
Three hymns sound like a rite happening as we listen.
The other three tell birth stories and great deeds.
Scholars read them mainly as learned poems for readers.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Miles Gloriosus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 205 BCE (Sort Year: -205)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Plautus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A vain soldier is tricked by a clever slave and loses the woman he stole.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: 205 BCE matches Britannica, which says the comedy was written about 205 BCE. Wikipedia treats it as an early play and links two lines to the imprisonment of Naevius in 206 BCE. No ancient notice gives an exact premiere day.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Pyrgopolynices (The braggart soldier, vain, lustful, and easily fooled); Palaestrio (The clever slave who designs both tricks); Philocomasium (The young woman kidnapped by the soldier); Pleusicles (Her lover, who comes to Ephesus to rescue her); Acroteleutium (The hired woman who pretends to desire the soldier)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Pyrgopolynices boasts of battles, while a parasite flatters him for meals.
He has carried Philocomasium from Athens to Ephesus.
The slave Palaestrio cuts a hole in the wall so she can meet Pleusicles.
They pretend she has a twin, then hire a woman to lure the soldier.
The soldier is beaten and robbed of his pride, and the lovers escape.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Menaechmi

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 200–190 BCE (Sort Year: -200)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Plautus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Twin brothers, long separated, cause a day of confusion in Epidamnus.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: No ancient production notice fixes the year. Wikipedia places the premiere in the late 3rd century BCE. The database range c. 200-190 BCE is a scholarly estimate. Curriculum lists often use c. 200 BCE. The sure Plautus dates are Stichus in 200 and Pseudolus in 191, not this play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Menaechmus of Epidamnus (The twin who lives in Epidamnus and cheats his wife); Menaechmus of Syracuse (The visiting twin, once called Sosicles, who is mistaken for his brother); Messenio (The loyal slave of the Syracusan twin); Erotium (The courtesan next door, who expects the local twin); The wife (The jealous wife of the Epidamnus twin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
One twin is stolen as a child and raised in Epidamnus.
The other twin, given the same name, arrives from Syracuse to search for him.
A courtesan, a parasite, and a wife each greet the wrong brother.
The visitor is thought mad, and the husband is nearly carried off as insane.
The brothers meet, the slave Messenio is freed, and the Epidamnus twin plans to leave.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Amphitryon

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 190 BCE (Sort Year: -190)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Plautus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jupiter disguises himself as Amphitryon, and the real husband cannot prove who he is.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: 190 BCE fits the scholarly range. Wikipedia, following recent editors, places the play probably in 190 to 185 BCE, late in Plautus's career. The exact festival is not recorded. A passage may refer to the Bacchanalia decree of 186 BCE, so some scholars prefer 186 to 185.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jupiter (The god who takes Amphitryon's shape); Mercury (Jupiter's son, disguised as the slave Sosia); Amphitryon (The Theban general who returns to a stolen identity); Alcmena (His faithful wife, deceived by the disguise); Sosia (Amphitryon's slave, who meets his own double)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Amphitryon and his slave Sosia are away at war.
Jupiter, disguised as Amphitryon, spends the night with Alcmena.
Mercury, disguised as Sosia, beats the real Sosia and denies his name.
Amphitryon returns, finds Alcmena already welcomed, and accuses her.
Alcmena gives birth to twins, and Jupiter explains that one son is Hercules.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Andria

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 166 BCE (Sort Year: -166)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Terence

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Terence's first play: a young man loves the girl from Andros, and a trick wedding almost ruins him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and the ancient production notice place the first performance at the Megalensian Games in 166 BCE. It is Terence's first produced play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Pamphilus (A young Athenian who loves Glycerium and fears his father's wedding plan); Simo (His father, who stages a false wedding to test him); Davus (A clever slave whose advice goes wrong); Glycerium (The girl from Andros, later found to be Chremes's daughter)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Pamphilus loves Glycerium, the girl from Andros, who is pregnant.
His father Simo pretends that a wedding to Philumena will happen that day.
The slave Davus tells Pamphilus to agree, hoping the other father will refuse.
The plan fails, and Pamphilus is trapped by his own consent.
Crito arrives and proves Glycerium is a free Athenian, so the true marriages can follow.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Eunuch

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 161 BCE (Sort Year: -161)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Terence

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Terence's greatest stage success: a youth disguises himself as a eunuch to enter a courtesan's house.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates the first performance to the Megalesian Games in 161 BCE. Suetonius says it earned a record price and was staged twice in one day.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Chaerea (A young man who disguises himself as the eunuch Dorus); Phaedria (His older brother, in love with Thais); Thais (A courtesan who tries to restore Pamphila to her family); Thraso (A braggart soldier and rival lover); Parmeno (The family slave who suggests the disguise)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Phaedria loves the courtesan Thais and agrees to leave town for two days.
His brother Chaerea sees Pamphila and, with the slave Parmeno, dresses as a eunuch.
Chaerea enters the house and assaults Pamphila, a citizen stolen as a child.
Pamphila is recognized as free born, and Chaerea agrees to marry her.
Phaedria keeps Thais, while the braggart soldier Thraso is allowed to help pay her costs.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Brothers

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 160 BCE (Sort Year: -160)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Terence

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A debate between a strict father and a lenient father about how to raise sons.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia places the first performance in 160 BCE at the funeral games of Aemilius Paullus. It is Terence's last play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Demea (The strict country father of Aeschinus and Ctesipho); Micio (The easy town brother who has adopted Aeschinus); Aeschinus (The elder son, raised by Micio, who helps his brother and loves Pamphila); Ctesipho (The younger son, raised strictly, who loves a music girl); Syrus (Micio's clever slave, who misleads Demea)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Demea raises Ctesipho strictly, while his brother Micio raises Aeschinus gently.
Aeschinus seizes a music girl for Ctesipho and takes the blame.
The slave Syrus sends Demea on false errands to hide Ctesipho.
Aeschinus has also promised marriage to Pamphila, who gives birth.
Demea then acts generous in order to expose Micio, and the sons accept Demea's guidance.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Poems / Carmina

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 60-54 BCE (Sort Year: -60)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Catullus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A book of about 116 poems, best known for the lyrics to Lesbia.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The poems themselves point to about 60 to 54 BCE. They mention his trip to Bithynia in 57 and 56 BCE. The surviving book comes from a manuscript found at Verona in 1305.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Catullus (The speaker of the personal poems); Lesbia (The beloved woman in the love lyrics, a poetic name); Juventius (A youth addressed in some of the love poems)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book mixes short poems, a few long ones, and elegiac epigrams.
The Lesbia poems tell joy, kisses, betrayal, hate, and love together.
Other poems attack Caesar and rivals, or joke with friends.
Poems 61 and 62 are marriage songs.
Poem 64 is a short epic on Peleus and Thetis.
Poem 101 mourns his brother at a grave in the Troad.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: De Oratore

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 55 BCE (Sort Year: -55)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Cicero

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A three book dialogue on the ideal orator, who joins skill in speech with wide knowledge.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Cicero finished this three book dialogue in 55 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lucius Licinius Crassus (A great Roman orator who defends a widely educated speaker); Marcus Antonius (A leading orator of the older generation, not the later Mark Antony); Quintus Mucius Scaevola (A legal expert who questions how far oratory should reach)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Cicero wrote the dialogue in 55 BCE and addressed it to his brother Quintus.
The scene is the villa of Crassus at Tusculum in 91 BCE.
Crassus and Antonius lead a talk on what makes a great speaker.
The ideal orator must know law, history, and ethics, not tricks alone.
Cicero says such a speaker can guide the state, so his character matters.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: De Republica

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 51 BCE (Sort Year: -51)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Cicero

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A six book dialogue on the best Roman state, ending with the Dream of Scipio.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He wrote the six books in those years. A reference book gives 52 BCE as one finish year inside that span. Much of the text was lost until a Vatican copy was found in 1819.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Scipio Aemilianus (The wise leader who explains Rome's constitution and tells the dream); Gaius Laelius (Scipio's close friend and partner in the discussion); Philus (A speaker who presents hard arguments about justice in Book 3)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Cicero wrote the six books between 54 and 51 BCE, imitating Plato.
Scipio Aemilianus leads a talk set long before Cicero's own day.
The speakers compare kingship, rule by the few, and rule by the people.
Cicero praises Rome's mixed constitution, which uses all three forms.
In the last book, Scipio tells a dream about duty, glory, and the soul.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: De Rerum Natura

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: by 54 BCE (Sort Year: -54)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Lucretius

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A six book poem that explains the world by atoms and tries to end the fear of death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Cicero mentioned the poem in a letter of 54 BCE. The sudden ending at the plague of Athens makes many scholars call it unfinished.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lucretius (The poet teacher who explains Epicurean philosophy); Memmius (The Roman addressed in the poem, likely Gaius Memmius); Venus (Addressed at the opening as a figure of nature's creative power)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lucretius addresses Venus, then turns to nature and attacks superstition.
Books 1 and 2 teach that atoms move in an endless void.
Book 3 says the soul dies with the body, so death is nothing to feel.
Book 4 explains the senses, dreams, and love.
Book 5 explains the world and human society.
Book 6 explains storms and disease, then ends with the plague at Athens.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Brutus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 46 BCE (Sort Year: -46)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Cicero

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dialogue in which Cicero gives Brutus and Atticus a history of Roman oratory.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database calls this work poetry, but it is a prose dialogue. It is a history of Roman speakers, not a poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Cicero (The main speaker, who surveys Roman orators and defends his style); Marcus Junius Brutus (The friend who asks Cicero to describe the great speakers); Titus Pomponius Atticus (Cicero's old friend, who speaks least of the three)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Cicero wrote the dialogue in 46 BCE, after the death of Hortensius.
Brutus and Atticus ask him to judge the great Roman speakers.
He begins with Greek oratory, then moves through Roman history.
He says many good speakers have gone silent in the civil war.
The book defends his own richer style against plainer Attic taste.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: De Officiis

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 44 BCE (Sort Year: -44)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Cicero

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A three book letter to his son on moral duty, advantage, and the clash between them.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Cicero wrote it in October and November 44 BCE, as a letter to his son. He was killed the next year, in 43 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Cicero (The writer, giving moral advice in the form of a letter); Marcus Cicero (Cicero's son, the student in Athens to whom the books are addressed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Cicero wrote the three books in October and November 44 BCE.
He addressed them to his son Marcus, who was studying in Athens.
Book 1 asks what is honorable, using the Stoic Panaetius as a guide.
Book 2 asks what is useful in public life and in gaining support.
Book 3 says the honorable and the useful never truly conflict.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Eclogues

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 39-38 BCE (Sort Year: -39)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Virgil

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ten pastoral poems on shepherds, song, love, and lost land.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica dates composition to 42-37 BCE. Wikipedia places publication near 39 to 38 BCE. The database shows 42-39 BCE. The exam span follows Britannica.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tityrus (A shepherd who keeps his land after a visit to Rome); Meliboeus (A shepherd driven off his farm); Corydon (A herdsman who sings of unreturned love); Gallus (A real elegiac poet, imagined dying of love in Arcadia)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Shepherds sing in an ideal countryside called Arcadia.
Some have lost farms after the civil wars.
Corydon sings of love that is not returned.
Eclogue 4 hopes a child will bring back a golden age.
The last poem places the poet Gallus in that pastoral world.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Satires

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 35-30 BCE (Sort Year: -35)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Horace

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Verse talks, also called Sermones, that mock folly in a friendly voice.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Book 1 appeared about 35 BCE, and Book 2 about 30 BCE. Wikipedia and the Poetry Foundation agree. The database records the same two dates.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Horace (The speaker, a freedman's son who laughs at folly and at himself); Maecenas (Horace's patron and the addressee of several satires)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Horace writes conversational hexameter poems on greed, sex, and friendship.
He claims Lucilius as the Roman founder of satire, then criticizes his rough style.
Book 1 includes the journey to Brundisium with Maecenas and Virgil.
Book 2 lets other speakers lecture, including the tale of the town mouse and the country mouse.
The laugh is gentle.
He ridicules types more than powerful living enemies.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Aeneid

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: after 19 BCE (Sort Year: -19)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Virgil

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unfinished epic of Aeneas leaving Troy to found the Roman people.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates the writing to 29-19 BCE. Britannica starts it about 30 BCE and says it was unfinished in 19 BCE. Varius and Tucca published it after Virgil died.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
