fields.value: Aeneas (A Trojan prince destined to begin the Roman line); Dido (Queen of Carthage, who loves Aeneas and then dies); Turnus (The Italian champion whom Aeneas kills at the end); Anchises (Aeneas' father, who reveals Rome's future among the dead); Juno (The goddess who opposes Aeneas through most of the poem)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A storm drives Aeneas to Carthage, where Dido loves him.
He tells of Troy's fall and his wanderings at sea.
He leaves Dido, and she kills herself.
In the underworld his father shows him future Romans.
In Italy he kills Turnus and ends the poem in grief.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Georgics

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 29 BCE (Sort Year: -29)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Virgil

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A four book poem that teaches farming and praises rural Italy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia says the poem was likely published in 29 BCE. Britannica dates the writing to 37 to 30 BCE. The database year 29 BCE is kept as the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet (The teacher who addresses Maecenas and the farmer); Maecenas (Virgil's patron, named at the start of the books); Aristaeus (A keeper of bees who learns how to restore his hive); Orpheus (The singer who looks back and loses Eurydice)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Book 1 teaches crops, weather, and the need for hard work.
Book 2 turns to trees, vines, and praise of Italy.
Book 3 treats cattle, horses, and a deadly animal plague.
Book 4 teaches beekeeping and tells of Aristaeus.
Inside that story, Orpheus fails to bring Eurydice back.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Metamorphoses

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 8 CE (Sort Year: -27)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ovid

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Fifteen books of myths about bodies changed into new forms.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates the poem to 8 CE. It was finished near the year Augustus exiled Ovid.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Daphne (A nymph who becomes a laurel tree to escape Apollo); Arachne (A weaver whom Minerva changes into a spider); Orpheus (A singer who loses Eurydice and then is killed); Pygmalion (A sculptor whose statue is brought to life); Julius Caesar (The Roman leader whose soul becomes a star at the end)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a narrative poem beginning with the creation of the world and ends in Ovid's time.
It consists of adventures of love affairs of deities and heroes.
More than 200 tales are taken from Greek and Roman Mythology, and these were the greatest source of Mythology for Renaissance writers.
The poem starts with creation, the ages, and the great flood.
Gods pursue mortals, and people become trees, birds, or stones.
Famous tales include Daphne, Echo, and Arachne.
Later books reach Troy, Aeneas, and early Rome.
It ends with Julius Caesar made a god, and with praise of Augustus.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Heroides

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 15 BCE (Sort Year: -15)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ovid

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Verse letters from mythic heroines to the men who left them.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia places the single letters between about 25 and 16 BCE. One passage may point to 19 BCE. About 15 BCE marks the late end of that range. Later paired letters are disputed.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Penelope (Odysseus' wife, writing while she waits at home); Dido (Queen of Carthage, writing to Aeneas after he leaves); Briseis (The captive woman writing to Achilles); Medea (The sorceress writing to Jason after his betrayal)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Famous women write to absent or unfaithful lovers.
Penelope writes to Odysseus, and Dido writes to Aeneas.
Each letter borrows a story from epic or tragedy.
The first set is 14 or 15 single letters.
Six later paired letters answer one another, and their authorship is disputed.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Odes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 23 BCE and 13 BCE (Sort Year: -23)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Horace

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Latin lyric poems, also called Carmina, on love, the state, wine, and death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Books 1 to 3 were published in 23 BCE. Book 4 followed the emperor's return from Spain in 13 BCE. Wikipedia places Book 4 about 11 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Horace (The lyric speaker, shifting between private joy and public praise); Maecenas (The patron addressed in the opening ode)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Horace adapts Greek lyric meters, especially Alcaic and Sapphic stanzas.
Books 1 to 3 move from private pleasures to public poems on Rome.
He tells the reader to seize the day because time will not wait.
The Roman Odes in Book 3 preach old virtues of simplicity and duty.
Book 4, written later, praises Augustus and the power of poetry to preserve fame.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Epistles

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 20-14 BCE (Sort Year: -20)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Horace

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Verse letters on how to live, how to treat patrons, and how to judge poetry.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Book 1 is about 21 to 19 BCE. The Poetry Foundation says 20 or early 19 BCE. The database says about 20 BCE. Book 2 is later. The database says about 13 BCE, and Wikipedia says about 11 BCE. The exam span used here is 20 to 14 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Horace (The letter writer, a poet turning toward moral questions); Maecenas (The patron addressed in several letters of Book 1); Augustus (The emperor addressed in the first letter of Book 2)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Horace says he is setting poetry aside to ask what is true and fitting.
Book 1 writes to friends about independence, place, and contentment.
He warns that a new sky does not give you a new mind.
Book 2 includes a long letter to Augustus on old and new Roman poets.
Another letter, to Florus, explains why good poems are hard to write.

items.title: "Ars Poetica / Epistle to the Pisones" (c. 19-18 BCE) — Horace

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Ars Poetica / Epistle to the Pisones

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 19-18 BCE (Sort Year: -19)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Horace

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A verse letter to the Piso family on how poems and plays should be made.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The traditional date is about 19 BCE. The database says about 19 to 18 BCE, and the year is uncertain. Wikipedia notes dates from 19 to 10 BCE. The Poetry Foundation also records a later guess, about 13 to 8 BCE. The exam date used here is about 19 to 18 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Horace (The poet giving practical advice in a verse letter); The Pisos (A father and two sons, the addressees of the epistle)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Horace tells the Pisos that a poem must be one whole, not a monster of mixed parts.
He warns against purple patches, showy lines sewn onto a plain poem.
Style and character must follow decorum, what is fitting.
He praises Homer for starting in the middle of things, in medias res.
He says poets wish to be useful and sweet, dulce et utile.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Amores

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 16 BCE (Sort Year: -16)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ovid

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three books of playful love elegies about the poet and Corinna.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The first edition, in five books, is dated to 16 BCE. The surviving text has three books. Scholars date that shorter edition to about 8 to 3 BCE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The lover (Ovid's playful speaker, not a plain record of his life); Corinna (The mistress of the poems, likely an invented figure); Cupid (The god who turns the poet from epic to love elegy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poet plans a war epic, but Cupid steals a metrical foot.
He falls for Corinna and writes scenes from the affair.
He jokes about rivals, gifts, a locked door, and a dead parrot.
Tragedy and Elegy argue over him in the last book.
He says farewell to love elegy at the end.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Ars Amatoria

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 2 BCE (Sort Year: -2)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Ovid

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A mock textbook in three books that teaches the arts of seduction.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia and World History Encyclopedia date the poem to 2 CE. Books 1 and 2 may be a little earlier than Book 3.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The teacher of love (Ovid's speaker, who claims to teach seduction); Venus (The goddess invoked as patron of the art)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Book 1 tells men where to find a lover in Rome.
Book 2 tells men how to keep her.
Book 3 gives women matching advice.
Mythic stories break up the witty rules.
Ovid later tied this poem to the cause of his exile.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Agamemnon

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1st century CE (Sort Year: 50)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Seneca

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tragedy in which Clytemnestra and Aegisthus murder Agamemnon on his return from Troy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database is right that the exact year is uncertain. The play belongs to the 1st century CE, before Seneca died in 65. Scholars place it after 40 CE and before 65 CE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Agamemnon (The king of Argos, killed after his victory at Troy); Clytemnestra (His wife, who plots the murder with her lover); Aegisthus (Son of Thyestes and Clytemnestra's partner in the killing); Cassandra (A captive princess from Troy who is ordered to die)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The ghost of Thyestes tells his son Aegisthus to take revenge.
Clytemnestra hates Agamemnon for killing their daughter Iphigenia.
She is also jealous because he brings Cassandra home from Troy.
She and Aegisthus murder Agamemnon when he returns.
Clytemnestra then orders death for Cassandra.

items.title: "Epigrams" (c. 86–102 CE; books published over time) — Martial

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Epigrams

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 86–102 CE; books published over time (Sort Year: 14)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Martial

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: More than 1,500 short poems on Roman city life, published from 80 to about 102 CE.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database starts the Epigrams at about 86 CE. That misses On the Spectacles, published in 80 CE for the Colosseum. Books 1 to 12 then appeared from 86 CE to about 102 CE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Martial (The poet speaker, often a client asking patrons for notice or gifts)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
On the Spectacles, in 80 CE, marks shows at the new Colosseum.
Two gift books, later numbered 13 and 14, appeared in 84 or 85 CE.
Books 1 and 2 came out in 86 CE, and later books followed almost yearly.
Most poems are elegiac couplets about real city types, with a joke at the end.
Book 12 was written in Spain and published about 102 CE.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Institutio Oratoria

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 95 CE (Sort Year: 14)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Quintilian

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A twelve book guide to educating the orator from infancy to retirement.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Both a standard encyclopedia and a detailed life place the twelve books near the end of his life.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Quintilian (The teacher speaking as the author of the whole course)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Quintilian published the twelve books near the end of his life, about 95 CE.
Books 1 and 2 cover education before the advanced school of rhetoric.
Books 3 to 11 teach invention, arrangement, style, memory, and delivery.
Book 10 surveys Greek and Latin authors whom the young speaker should read.
Book 12 says the finished orator must be a good citizen who serves the public.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Medea

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1st century CE (Sort Year: 50)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Seneca

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tragedy in which Medea kills to punish Jason for leaving her.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database is right that the exact year is uncertain. The play is a 1st century CE work from Seneca's lifetime. Some scholars place it around 50 CE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Medea (A princess and witch who speaks more than half the play); Jason (Her husband, who abandons her for a royal marriage); Creon (King of Corinth, father of Creusa, killed by the poisoned robe); Creusa (Jason's new bride, burned by Medea's gift)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jason leaves Medea to marry Creusa, daughter of King Creon.
Creon gives Medea one day before he sends her into exile.
Medea sends a poisoned robe as a wedding gift.
The robe burns Creusa, and Creon dies with her.
Medea kills her sons, then flies away in a dragon chariot.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Oedipus

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1st century CE (Sort Year: 50)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Seneca

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tragedy of Oedipus discovering that he killed his father and married his mother.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database is right that the exact year is uncertain. The play belongs to the 1st century CE, before Seneca died in 65. A scholarly table places it after 40 CE and before 65 CE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Oedipus (King of Thebes, who learns the truth of his birth and his crime); Jocasta (Queen of Thebes, wife and mother of Oedipus); Creon (Brother of Jocasta, who brings the oracle and the ghost's message); Tiresias (The blind prophet who seeks the killer through sacrifice and a ghost)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A plague strikes Thebes while Oedipus is king.
The oracle says the city must avenge the dead king Laius.
Tiresias calls up the ghost of Laius to name the killer.
Oedipus learns that he killed Laius and that Jocasta is his mother.
Oedipus blinds himself, and Jocasta kills herself.

items.title: "Parallel Lives" (c. 100–120 CE; individual lives vary) — Plutarch

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Parallel Lives

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 100–120 CE; individual lives vary (Sort Year: 14)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Plutarch

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Paired biographies of Greek and Roman leaders, written to display character and noble deeds.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database span about 100 to 120 CE fits the later years of his life. Individual lives vary. The English book that matters for exams is Sir Thomas North's translation, first printed in 1579.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Plutarch (The biographer who compares each Greek and Roman pair); Alexander and Julius Caesar (A famous pair of conquerors in the Lives); Demosthenes and Cicero (A famous pair of orators in the Lives)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Plutarch pairs a famous Greek with a famous Roman.
He tells birth, character, deeds, and death for each person.
A short comparison follows most pairs.
He wants readers to copy noble conduct, not only to learn facts.
North's English version of 1579 supplied Shakespeare with Roman plots.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Phaedra

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1st century CE (Sort Year: 50)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Seneca

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tragedy of Phaedra's desire for her stepson Hippolytus and the deaths that follow.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database is right that the exact year is uncertain. One chronology places the play before 54 CE. It is still safely a 1st century CE work of Seneca's lifetime.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Phaedra (Wife of Theseus, who openly pursues her stepson); Hippolytus (Son of Theseus, who rejects Phaedra and is later killed); Theseus (King of Athens, whose curse destroys his son); The Nurse (Phaedra's servant, drawn into the scheme)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Theseus is away, and his wife Phaedra desires his son Hippolytus.
She tells Hippolytus of her love, and he runs away in horror.
Phaedra accuses Hippolytus of trying to attack her.
Theseus curses his son, and Hippolytus is killed.
Phaedra kills herself, and Theseus learns the truth too late.

items.title: "Satires" (c. 100–127 CE; books published over time) — Juvenal

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Satires

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 100–127 CE; books published over time (Sort Year: 14)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Juvenal

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Sixteen satires in five books that attack the vices of imperial Rome.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database range of about 100 to 127 CE matches the book dates. Book 1 came out between 100 and 110 CE. The last book refers to events of 127 CE. Together these years are the early 2nd century CE.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The satiric speaker (An angry voice that attacks Rome's vices); Umbricius (A friend in Satire 3 who leaves Rome for a quiet town)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Book 1, Satires 1 to 5, looks back at Domitian and came out between 100 and 110 CE.
Satire 1 says vice is so bad that it is hard not to write satire.
Satire 6 attacks Roman women and asks who will guard the guards.
Satire 10 rejects vain wishes and praises a sound mind in a sound body.
The last book refers to 127 CE, and Satire 16 breaks off in mid sentence.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Thyestes

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1st century CE (Sort Year: 50)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Seneca

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tragedy in which Atreus kills the sons of Thyestes and serves them to their father.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database is right that the exact year is uncertain. The play is a 1st century CE tragedy from Seneca's lifetime. Later English revenge plays took it as a model.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Atreus (King who plans a cannibal feast as revenge); Thyestes (The brother who returns from exile and eats the fatal meal); The Ghost of Tantalus (An ancestor whose curse hangs over the house); The Messenger (Reports the secret murder of the three sons)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Atreus and Thyestes are brothers who both want their father's throne.
Thyestes steals a golden ram and is banished.
Atreus pretends to forgive him and calls him home.
Atreus kills the three sons and serves them at a feast.
Atreus then shows Thyestes what he has eaten.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: On the Sublime

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1554 (Sort Year: 1554)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Longinus

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Greek treatise on the sublime, the power of great writing to transport a reader.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Wikipedia place the work in the 1st century CE. The database says the date and the author are disputed. The Greek text was first printed in 1554. Wikipedia records Boileau's French translation in 1674, and Britannica confirms that Boileau translated it.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Longinus (The unknown author, often called Pseudo-Longinus); Postumius Terentianus (The Roman friend to whom the treatise is addressed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The author writes to Terentianus about what makes style truly high.
Sublimity does not merely persuade.
It carries the hearer into ecstasy.
Two sources are inborn: great thoughts and strong feeling.
Three sources are learned: figures, noble diction, and dignified word order.
He illustrates the sublime from Homer, Plato, Sappho, and Genesis.

items.title: "Moralia" (1st–2nd century CE; collection assembled over tim) — Plutarch

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Moralia

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 1st–2nd century CE; collection assembled over tim (Sort Year: 150)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Plutarch

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A large set of essays and dialogues on ethics, religion, politics, and literature.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It is not one book from a single year. The essays belong to the first and second centuries CE. They were written across his later life, from about 100 CE onward.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Plutarch (The essayist and usual speaker of the moral pieces)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Moralia gather more than sixty essays and dialogues.
Topics include ethics, religion, politics, and how to read poets.
Some pieces are talks among Plutarch's family and friends.
He quotes earlier Greek poets to test a moral point.
The collection grew over many years, not in one sitting.

items.title: "Christian apologetic works" (c. 197–220 CE; individual works vary) — Tertullian

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Christian apologetic works

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: c. 197–220 CE; individual works vary (Sort Year: 180)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Tertullian

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Latin defenses of Christianity, above all the Apologeticus of 197, addressed to Roman governors.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database span c. 197-220 covers his whole writing life. The Apologeticus and Ad nationes belong to 197. The Catholic Encyclopedia and the Tertullian Project agree on that year. Later moral and Montanist tracts fall after 200. The database calls the group Poetry. That label is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tertullian (The speaker, a Christian advocate addressing Roman officials); The Roman governors (The officials asked to judge Christians by reason and law)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tertullian writes to Roman governors in 197.
He says Christians are punished for the name alone, without proved crimes.
He denies that Christians cause disasters or refuse loyalty to the emperor.
He explains belief in one God and in Christ.
He describes a church that prays for rulers and gives help to the poor.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Confessions

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 400 (Sort Year: 400)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: St. Augustine

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A spiritual autobiography in 13 books, written as a prayer to God.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates the 13 books to 397 to 400. Britannica dates the finished work about 400. It circulated in manuscript, not in print.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Augustine (The speaker, who tells his sins and his conversion as a prayer); Monica (His Christian mother, who dies at Ostia after his baptism); Ambrose (Bishop of Milan, whose preaching draws Augustine toward the church); Alypius (A close friend who is baptized with Augustine)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Augustine recalls his childhood, a theft of pears, and years of desire.
He follows the Manichees (a group who split good and evil into two powers), then doubts them.
In Milan he hears Bishop Ambrose and begins to read Paul.
In a garden a childlike voice says, Take up and read, and he converts.
He is baptized, his mother Monica dies, and later books discuss memory, time, and Genesis.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Latin Vulgate Bible — translation/revision

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 405 (Sort Year: 405)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Jerome

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jerome's revision and translation of the Bible into Latin, later called the Vulgate.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database span c. 382-405 is correct for the project as a whole. Britannica dates the Gospel revision about 383 and the Hebrew Old Testament about 405. The Catholic Encyclopedia dates the Gospel correction to 384 and the Hebrew version from 390 to 405. The books were copied by hand. The name Vulgate became usual later.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jerome (The scholar who revised and translated the Latin biblical text); Pope Damasus I (The pope who commissioned the revision in 382)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 382 Pope Damasus asked Jerome to revise the old Latin Bible.
Jerome revised the four Gospels from Greek copies about 383.
He first made some Old Testament books from the Greek Septuagint.
He then translated the Old Testament from Hebrew and finished about 405.
Much of the rest of the New Testament remained in older Latin versions.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The City of God

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 426 (Sort Year: 426)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: St. Augustine

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long defense of Christianity written after the Visigoths sacked Rome in 410.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Britannica and Wikipedia agree that he wrote it after 410 and finished the whole work in 426. It was issued in parts over those years.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Augustine (The author, who argues against pagan blame of Christianity); The City of God (The community of those who love God above the self); The earthly city (The community of those who love self and worldly glory)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Pagans blamed the sack of Rome in 410 on the Christian faith.
Augustine answers that Rome fell through its own moral decay.
He describes two cities, one formed by love of God and one by love of self.
The first 10 books answer pagan religion and pagan philosophy.
The last 12 books retell history from creation to the Last Judgment.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Consolation of Philosophy

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 524 (Sort Year: 524)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Boethius

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prison dialogue in which Lady Philosophy comforts the condemned Boethius.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: 523-524 matches the prison years. Britannica dates the book about 524, while he was under sentence of death. Stanford says he wrote it in prison before execution, which Britannica and Wikipedia date to 524. It was copied in manuscript. There was no print edition in his lifetime.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Boethius (The prisoner who complains and then learns); Lady Philosophy (A personified teacher who consoles him with argument and verse); Fortune (The changing power whose wheel lifts people and then casts them down)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Boethius sits in prison and grieves for his lost office and fame.
Lady Philosophy appears and sends away the Muses of mere poetry.
She shows that riches, high rank, and power are unstable goods.
She teaches that true happiness is God, the highest good.
In Book 5 she treats free will together with God's knowledge of the future.

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Socrates

fields.label: Publication / Composition Date
fields.value: 0 (Sort Year: 0)

fields.label: Author
fields.value: Socrates

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(470 - 399 BC)
Socrates was a classical Greek Philosopher credited as one of the founders of Western Philosophy.
He is an enigmatic figure chiefly known through the accounts of classical writers especially the writings of his students Plato and Xenophon and the plays of his contemporary Aristophanes.
Socrates has become renowned for his contribution to the field of Ethics and it is this Platonic Socrates who lends his name to the concept of Socratic Irony and the Socratic Method.
Socrates also made important and lasting contributions to the field of Epistemology.
Socrates never individually wrote anything that remains extant. As a result, all first-hand information about him and his philosophies depend upon secondary sources. This issue is known as Socratic Problem or Socratic Question.
To understand Socrates one must turn primarily to the works of Plato, whose dialogues are thought the most informative source about Socrates' life and philosophy and also Xenophon. These writings are the Socratikoilogoi or Socratic Dialogue which consists of reports of conversations apparently involving Socrates.
He was prominently lampooned in Aristophanes' comedy "The Clouds".
In comedy entitled "The Clouds" ancient Greek author Aristophanes pokes fun at Socrates.
